title: Family, possession and the genitive
objectives: I can name the members of my family and say who has children.
I can say what I have and do not have with 'у ме́не є' and 'у ме́не нема́є'.
I can form the genitive singular of nouns, adjectives and possessive pronouns, and choose between '-а' and '-у' for a masculine noun.
I can say whose something is with the genitive and with 'чий', 'чия́', 'чиє́' and 'чиї́'.
I can use 'без', 'для', 'бі́ля', 'з' and 'до' with the genitive, and address the members of my family in the vocative.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'ба́тька', vocative 'ба́тьку'. A masculine noun in '-о', like 'та́то'. It is the neutral word, used in writing and in respectful talk about someone's father; in the family, 'та́то' is usual. Its plural 'батьки́' also means 'parents'.

example.source: My father works at a bank.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'ма́тері'; the genitive and most other forms are built on the stem 'ма́тер-'. The neutral word, like 'ба́тько'; in the family, 'ма́ма' is usual. The verb 'ма́ти', to have, is a different word with the same spelling.
Genitive 'до́ньки', vocative 'до́нько'. Parents often call a daughter 'до́нько' instead of by her name.
Genitive 'бабу́сі', vocative 'бабу́сю'. An affectionate form of 'ба́ба' and the usual word in the family, like 'Grandma'.
Genitive 'діду́ся', vocative 'діду́сю'. An affectionate form of 'дід' and the usual word in the family, like 'Grandpa'.

example.source: My grandpa is sitting in the park.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'чолові́ка'. With a possessive, as in 'мій чолові́к', it means 'husband'; without one it usually means 'man'. The adjective 'чолові́чий', masculine, comes from it.

example.source: Her husband works at a school.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'дружи́ни'. It is built on the same root as 'друг', friend.

example.source: His wife works at a pharmacy.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'дити́ни'. It is feminine whether the child is a boy or a girl: 'на́ша дити́на'. Its plural is 'ді́ти'.
The plural of 'дити́на', built on another stem: the singular has the suffix '-ин-', which the plural lacks.
The plural of 'ба́тько', with the stress on the ending. It means 'parents', and also 'fathers'.
Genitive 'дя́дька', vocative 'дя́дьку'. A masculine noun in '-о', like 'ба́тько'. Children also call any grown man they know 'дя́дьку'.

example.target: У ме́не є дя́дько в Кана́ді.
example.source: I have an uncle in Canada.
example.source_literal: At me is uncle in Canada.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'ті́тки', vocative 'ті́тко'. Children also call any grown woman they know 'ті́тко'.

example.source: My aunt works at the library.

vocabulary.source: there is not, there are not
vocabulary.note: It takes the genitive of what is absent. 'Нема́' is a shorter form with the same meaning. It grew out of 'не' and 'ма́є', has.
It takes the genitive. With a person it means to that person or to that person's home.
It takes the genitive and always has a noun or pronoun after it; the adverb 'по́руч', nearby, stands alone.

example.source: The pharmacy is next to the post office.

vocabulary.note: 'Чия́', 'чиє́', 'чиї́'. It agrees with the thing owned, like 'мій'.

dialogues.title: A family photo
dialogues.context: Sam visits Oksana at home. A big family photo hangs on the wall, and he asks who everyone is. They are friends and say 'ти'.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Окса́но, це твоя́ сім’я́?
lines.source: Oksana, is this your family?
lines.source_literal: Oksana, this your family?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Так. Ось мої́ батьки́, мій брат, бабу́ся й діду́сь.
lines.source: Yes. Here are my parents, my brother, Grandma and Grandpa.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А хто це бі́ля твоє́ї ма́ми?
lines.source: And who is that next to your mom?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Це моя́ ті́тка, сестра́ ма́ми. А це її́ чолові́к, мій дя́дько.
lines.source: That is my aunt, Mom's sister. And that is her husband, my uncle.
lines.source_literal: This my aunt, sister of-mom. And this her husband, my uncle.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: У них є ді́ти?
lines.source: Do they have children?
lines.source_literal: At them are children?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Так, у них є син і до́нька.
lines.source: Yes, they have a son and a daughter.
lines.source_literal: Yes, at them is son and daughter.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А твій брат? У ньо́го є ді́ти?
lines.source: And your brother? Does he have children?
lines.source_literal: And your brother? At him are children?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: У ньо́го є до́нька. Її́ зва́ти О́ля.
lines.source: He has a daughter. Her name is Olia.
lines.source_literal: At him is daughter. Her to-call Olia.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А де ти? Я тебе́ не ба́чу.
lines.source: And where are you? I don't see you.
lines.source_literal: And where you? I you not see.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Я ось тут, бі́ля діду́ся.
lines.source: I am right here, next to Grandpa.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Яка́ вели́ка сім’я́! А в ме́не нема́є бра́та чи сестри́.
lines.source: What a big family! And I don't have a brother or a sister.
lines.source_literal: What-kind big family! And at me there-is-not of-brother or of-sister.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Але́ в те́бе є дру́зі в Ки́єві!
lines.source: But you have friends in Kyiv!
lines.source_literal: But at you are friends in Kyiv!

dialogues.title: Lunch at home
dialogues.context: Sunday lunch at the home of Oksana's parents, Halyna and Mykola. The family says 'ти' to one another, and the parents call Oksana 'до́нько'.

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: Окса́но, до́нько, де ти? Борщ на столі́!
lines.source: Oksana, sweetheart, where are you? The borscht is on the table!
lines.source_literal: Oksana, daughter, where you? Borscht on table!

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Я тут, ма́мо! Я йду.
lines.source: I'm here, Mom! I'm coming.
lines.source_literal: I here, mom! I go.

lines.speaker: Мико́ла
lines.target: Гали́но, а де хліб? На столі́ нема́є хлі́ба.
lines.source: Halyna, where is the bread? There is no bread on the table.
lines.source_literal: Halyna, and where bread? On table there-is-not of-bread.

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: Хліб на ку́хні, бі́ля вікна́.
lines.source: The bread is in the kitchen, by the window.
lines.source_literal: Bread on kitchen, near window.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Та́ту, ось хліб.
lines.source: Dad, here is the bread.
lines.source_literal: Dad, here-is bread.

lines.speaker: Мико́ла
lines.target: Дя́кую, до́нько. А ти їси́ борщ без м’я́са?
lines.source: Thank you, sweetheart. Do you eat borscht without meat?
lines.source_literal: I-thank, daughter. And you eat borscht without meat?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Так, без м’я́са. Ма́мо, а для ме́не є ка́ва?
lines.source: Yes, without meat. Mom, is there coffee for me?
lines.source_literal: Yes, without meat. Mom, and for me is coffee?

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: Є, є. Ось ка́ва для те́бе. Без цу́кру, так?
lines.source: Yes, there is. Here is coffee for you. No sugar, right?
lines.source_literal: Is, is. Here-is coffee for you. Without sugar, yes?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Так, дя́кую. А де бабу́ся?
lines.source: Yes, thank you. And where is Grandma?
lines.source_literal: Yes, I-thank. And where grandma?

lines.speaker: Мико́ла
lines.target: Бабу́ся сього́дні в ті́тки.
lines.source: Grandma is at your aunt's today.
lines.source_literal: Grandma today at aunt.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: А діду́сь?
lines.source: And Grandpa?

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: Діду́сь у па́рку, бі́ля о́зера.
lines.source: Grandpa is in the park, by the lake.

lines.speaker: Мико́ла
lines.target: До́бре. Смачно́го, Окса́но!
lines.source: All right. Enjoy your meal, Oksana!
lines.source_literal: Well. Of-tasty, Oksana!

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Дя́кую, та́ту! Смачно́го, ма́мо!
lines.source: Thank you, Dad! Enjoy your meal, Mom!
lines.source_literal: I-thank, dad! Of-tasty, mom!

dialogues.title: Whose is this?
dialogues.context: Taras and his friends spent the evening at Andrii's café. After they leave, Andrii finds some things on their table and calls Taras, who comes back with his sister Olena. Andrii and his customers say 'ви' and use 'па́не' with the vocative of a first name.

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: Па́не Тара́се, тут на столі́ ключ, телефо́н і кни́га. Чий це ключ?
lines.source: Taras, there is a key, a phone and a book on the table here. Whose key is this?
lines.source_literal: Mr. Taras, here on table key, phone and book. Whose this key?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Це ключ Се́ма. За́раз він без ключа́!
lines.source: That is Sam's key. Now he has no key!
lines.source_literal: This key of-Sam. Now he without key!

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: І без телефо́ну! Це телефо́н Се́ма, я зна́ю.
lines.source: And no phone! That is Sam's phone, I know it.
lines.source_literal: And without phone! This phone of-Sam, I know.

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: А чия́ це кни́га?
lines.source: And whose book is this?
lines.source_literal: And whose this book?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Це кни́га Окса́ни. Ду́же ціка́ва кни́га.
lines.source: It is Oksana's book. A very interesting book.
lines.source_literal: This book of-Oksana. Very interesting book.

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: А чиї́ це ру́чки?
lines.source: And whose pens are these?
lines.source_literal: And whose this pens?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Це мої́ ру́чки! Дя́кую, па́не Андрі́ю.
lines.source: They are my pens! Thank you, Andrii.
lines.source_literal: This my pens! I-thank, Mr. Andrii.

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: Будь ла́ска. А чиє́ це я́блуко?
lines.source: You're welcome. And whose apple is this?
lines.source_literal: Be kindness. And whose this apple?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Не зна́ю. Це не моє́ я́блуко.
lines.source: I don't know. It is not my apple.
lines.source_literal: Not I-know. This not my apple.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: І не моє́. Я́блуко для вас, па́не Андрі́ю!
lines.source: Not mine either. The apple is for you, Andrii!
lines.source_literal: And not mine. Apple for you, Mr. Andrii!

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: Дя́кую! А ключ і телефо́н Се́ма?
lines.source: Thank you! And Sam's key and phone?
lines.source_literal: I-thank! And key and phone of-Sam?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: За́раз ми йдемо́ до Се́ма. Він живе́ бли́зько, бі́ля па́рку.
lines.source: We are going to Sam's now. He lives close by, near the park.
lines.source_literal: Now we go to Sam. He lives close, near park.

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: До́бре. До поба́чення!
lines.source: Good. Goodbye!
lines.source_literal: Well. Until seeing!

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: the family words
grammar.explanation:
Every new word in this unit can be read with the rules of the first four units. The points below are the ones these words show.

A soft sign inside a word softens the consonant before it, and that consonant stays soft before the next consonant:

- 'ба́тько' [ˈbɑtʲkɔ] has a soft 'т' before 'к', and the 'ь' stays in every form: 'ба́тька', 'ба́тьку'.
- 'дя́дько' [ˈdʲɑdʲkɔ] has two soft consonants: 'я' softens the first 'д' and 'ь' the second.
- 'до́нька' [ˈdɔnʲkɑ] has a soft 'н' before 'к'.

A soft consonant is written in two ways (unit 3): with 'ь' when a consonant or nothing follows, and with 'я', 'ю', 'є' or 'і' when a vowel follows. So a word can change its spelling while its consonant keeps the same sound:

- 'діду́сь' [dʲiˈdusʲ] ends in a soft [sʲ] written 'сь'. Its genitive 'діду́ся' and its vocative 'діду́сю' have the same soft 'с', now shown by 'я' and 'ю'.
- 'бабу́ся' [bɑˈbusʲɑ] keeps the same soft 'с' in 'бабу́сі' and 'бабу́сю'.

'Дити́на' [dɪˈtɪnɑ] and 'ді́ти' [ˈdʲitɪ] begin with the same letter but not the same sound: 'д' is hard before 'и' and soft before 'і'. In 'ті́тка' [ˈtʲitkɑ] the first 'т' is soft before 'і' and the second is hard before 'к'.

'Ма́ти', mother, has a stem extension: a piece of the stem that the nominative does not show and most other forms do. These forms are built on 'ма́тер-', so its genitive is 'ма́тері' [ˈmɑtɛrʲi]. Learn 'ма́ти' and 'ма́тері' as a pair. The verb 'ма́ти', to have, has the same spelling, and the note on having explains it; they are two different words.

An ending added to a noun can change its stem, and this unit's forms show these changes:

- 'і' in a closed last syllable returns to 'о' or 'е' when an ending opens the syllable: 'кіт', 'кота́'; 'стіл', 'стола́'; 'дім', 'до́му'; 'Львів', 'Льво́ва'. Feminine nouns in a consonant do the same: 'сіль', 'со́лі'; 'о́сінь', 'о́сені'.
- 'ї' after a vowel returns to 'є': 'Ки́їв', 'Ки́єва'.
- Some words lose the vowel of their last syllable when an ending is added: 'цу́кор', 'цу́кру'; 'ри́нок', 'ри́нку'; 'оліве́ць', 'олівця́'. Such a vowel is called a fleeting vowel (unit 12), and every form with an ending uses the stem without it.
- Before the vocative ending '-е', 'г' becomes 'ж' and 'к' becomes 'ч': 'друг', 'дру́же'; 'чолові́к', 'чолові́че'.

The genitive forms of the pronouns are read by the same rules. 'Ньо́го' [ˈnʲɔɦɔ] writes a soft 'н' plus 'о' with 'ьо' (unit 3), and 'не́ї' [ˈnɛji] ends in 'ї', which is always [ji]. In 'чия́' [t͡ʃɪˈjɑ], 'чиє́' [t͡ʃɪˈjɛ] and 'чиї́' [t͡ʃɪˈji] the vowel letters follow a vowel, so they begin with [j]. In 'нема́є' [nɛˈmɑjɛ] each unstressed 'е' moves toward 'и' (unit 4). 'Сім’ї́' [sʲimˈji], the genitive of 'сім’я́', keeps the apostrophe: the 'м' stays hard, and 'ї' is [ji].

Stress moves in many of these forms, and in this course's spelling the stress mark is the only written difference between some of them; ordinary print has no mark, so there the sentence decides:

- 'сестри́', of the sister, keeps the stress of 'сестра́' on the ending; 'се́стри', sisters, and the vocative 'се́стро' move it to the first syllable.
- 'вікна́', of the window, against 'ві́кна', windows.
- 'мі́ста', of the city, against 'міста́', cities.
- Some masculine nouns move the stress onto the ending: 'ключ', 'ключа́'; 'кіт', 'кота́'; 'борщ', 'борщу́'.

Learn each genitive with its mark.

rows: at the end of a word
the same soft с before a vowel

examples.target: Мій ба́тько й мій дя́дько тут.
examples.source: My father and my uncle are here.
The children are next to their mother.
My sister is not at home.

grammar.title: The genitive singular of nouns
grammar.explanation:
The genitive, 'родови́й відмі́нок' in Ukrainian grammar, answers the questions 'кого́?', of whom, and 'чого́?', of what. It does the work that English does with 'of' and with an apostrophe and 's'. Its main jobs at this level are these:

- naming the owner or the whole that something belongs to: 'кни́га Окса́ни', Oksana's book, literally 'book of-Oksana'
- naming what is absent, after 'нема́є': 'нема́є хлі́ба', there is no bread
- following many prepositions, among them 'у' in 'у ме́не є', and 'без', 'для', 'бі́ля', 'з' meaning 'from', and 'до'

You have met genitive forms already without the name. 'З Ки́єва' and 'з Кана́ди' (unit 7) are genitives after 'з'. The accusative of a masculine person or animal (unit 10), as in 'Я ба́чу бра́та', borrows its form from the genitive, so 'бра́та' is also the genitive of 'брат'.

The ending depends on the gender and on the stem. A hard stem ends in a hard consonant ('сестр-', 'брат'); a soft stem ends in a soft consonant or in 'й' ('бабу́с-', 'чай').

Feminine nouns:

- '-а' after a hard stem becomes '-и': 'ма́ма', 'ма́ми'; 'сестра́', 'сестри́'; 'кни́га', 'кни́ги'.
- '-я' after a soft stem becomes '-і': 'земля́', 'землі́'; 'бабу́ся', 'бабу́сі'; 'ку́хня', 'ку́хні'.
- After 'ж', 'ч', 'ш' and 'щ' the ending is '-і', as in the nominative plural (unit 8): 'пло́ща', 'пло́щі'; 'ї́жа', 'ї́жі'.
- After a vowel or an apostrophe, '-я' becomes '-ї': 'сім’я́', 'сім’ї́'; 'Со́фія', 'Со́фії'.
- A feminine noun in a consonant takes '-і': 'сіль', 'со́лі'; 'о́сінь', 'о́сені'.
- 'Ма́ти', mother, ends in '-и', but its genitive is built on the stem 'ма́тер-' and takes '-і', as a feminine noun in a consonant does: 'ма́тері'.

The genitive singular of a feminine noun often has the same letters as its nominative plural: 'кни́ги' means 'of the book' or 'books'. The sentence decides, and sometimes the stress does too: 'сестри́' against 'се́стри'.

Neuter nouns take '-а' where the nominative has '-о': 'мі́сто', 'мі́ста'; 'вікно́', 'вікна́'; 'молоко́', 'молока́'. Neuter nouns in '-я', such as 'життя́' and 'перехре́стя', keep the same letters in the genitive. Nouns that never change form ('кафе́', 'меню́', 'метро́') stay the same here too: 'бі́ля кафе́'.

Masculine nouns take '-а' or '-у' after a hard stem, and '-я' or '-ю' after a soft one: 'брат', 'бра́та'; 'суп', 'су́пу'; 'Андрі́й', 'Андрі́я'; 'чай', 'ча́ю'. A masculine noun in '-о' replaces it with the same endings: 'та́то', 'та́та'; 'ба́тько', 'ба́тька'. A masculine noun in '-а', such as 'Мико́ла', is still masculine but takes the endings of 'ма́ма': 'у Мико́ли'.

Choosing between '-а' and '-у' is the one hard part of the genitive singular. The choice follows the meaning of the noun:

- '-а' or '-я' for people and animals: 'бра́та', 'си́на', 'діду́ся', 'кота́'
- '-а' or '-я' for concrete things that are counted one by one: 'стола́', 'ключа́', 'олівця́'
- '-а' or '-я' for most cities: 'Ки́єва', 'Льво́ва'
- '-у' or '-ю' for substances: 'си́ру', 'ча́ю', 'цу́кру', 'со́ку', 'су́пу'
- '-у' or '-ю' for buildings, institutions and places: 'до́му', 'па́рку', 'магази́ну', 'університе́ту', 'музе́ю'
- '-у' or '-ю' for abstract ideas and for many words borrowed from other languages: 'ча́су', 'це́нтру', 'телефо́ну'

These groups are strong tendencies, not laws, and they can disagree: 'телефо́н' is a thing counted one by one, but as a borrowed word it takes '-у'. Some words follow none of them: 'хліб' names a substance but takes '-а', as in 'нема́є хлі́ба'. From this unit on, the vocabulary note of every new masculine noun gives its genitive, so learn the two forms together.

examples.source: The city center is far away.

examples.target: Я з Ки́єва, а Сем із Кана́ди.
examples.source: I am from Kyiv, and Sam is from Canada.

grammar.title: Whose: possession by a noun, 'чий' and adjectives in the genitive
grammar.explanation:
English names an owner in two ways: before the thing with an apostrophe and 's' ('Oksana's book'), or after it with 'of' ('the book of Oksana'). Ukrainian normally uses the second pattern. The thing comes first, and the owner follows it in the genitive:

- 'кни́га Окса́ни', Oksana's book, literally 'book of-Oksana'
- 'брат Тара́са', Taras's brother, literally 'brother of-Taras'
- 'центр мі́ста', the city center, literally 'center of-city'

The same order serves every relation that English expresses with an apostrophe and 's' or with 'of', not only ownership: 'ма́ти Оле́ни', Olena's mother.

To ask whose something is, use the interrogative pronoun 'чий', whose. Like 'мій' (unit 8), it agrees with the thing owned, never with the owner:

- 'чий' with a masculine noun: 'Чий це ключ?'
- 'чия́' with a feminine noun: 'Чия́ це кни́га?'
- 'чиє́' with a neuter noun: 'Чиє́ це я́блуко?'
- 'чиї́' with a plural: 'Чиї́ це ді́ти?'

In these questions 'це' is the pointing word of unit 8, and the answer keeps the same frame with the owner in the genitive: 'Це ключ Се́ма.', literally 'this key of-Sam'. In 'Чия́ це кни́га?' the form 'чия́' is feminine because 'кни́га' is feminine, even when the owner turns out to be a man.

An adjective or a possessive pronoun before a noun in the genitive is in the genitive too, because it agrees with the noun in gender, number and case (unit 5). There are only two endings to learn in the singular:

- '-ого' for masculine and neuter: 'вели́кого', 'на́шого'; after a soft stem '-ього': 'си́нього', 'ї́хнього'
- '-ої' for feminine: 'вели́кої', 'на́шої'; after a soft stem '-ьої': 'си́ньої', 'ї́хньої'

'Мій' and 'твій' have forms of their own: 'мого́', 'моє́ї'; 'твого́', 'твоє́ї'. An adjective stressed on its ending keeps the stress on the first vowel of the new ending: 'нови́й', 'ново́го', 'ново́ї'; 'стари́й', 'старо́го'. You have met '-ого' before: in 'ново́го дру́га' (unit 10) the accusative of a masculine person borrows it from the genitive, and 'Смачно́го!' is the genitive of 'смачни́й'.

'Його́', 'її́' and 'їх' never change, because they are already genitive forms of 'він', 'вона́' and 'вони́': 'його́ сестра́' is literally 'of-him sister'. So in 'телефо́н його́ сестри́', his sister's phone, only 'сестра́' changes.

grammar.title: Having, not having and the prepositions that take the genitive
grammar.explanation:
Ukrainian usually says what someone has with the preposition 'у' and the genitive of the owner: 'У ме́не є брат.', I have a brother, literally 'at me is brother'. Three things differ from English:

- The owner is not the subject. It follows 'у', in the genitive.
- The thing owned is the subject, in the nominative: 'брат'.
- The verb is 'є', the one present form of 'бу́ти', to be (unit 5), which states that something exists.

The owner can be a noun: 'У Тара́са є сестра́.', Taras has a sister. Euphony applies to 'у' as everywhere: 'В Оле́ни є брат.' at the start of a sentence before a vowel, and 'А в ме́не є сестра́.' after a vowel.

To say that something is absent, put 'нема́є' in place of 'є' and the missing thing in the genitive: 'У ме́не нема́є бра́та.', I don't have a brother, literally 'at me there-is-not of-brother'. 'Нема́є' is a predicative word (unit 10), a word that is the whole predicate of a sentence without a grammatical subject. Because the sentence has no subject, the missing thing cannot be in the nominative, and it takes the genitive. 'Нема́є' also says that someone is not in a place: 'Ма́ми нема́є вдо́ма.', Mom is not at home. The shorter 'нема́' means the same and is common in speech.

'Нема́є' grew out of 'не' and 'ма́є', has. 'Ма́є' is the 'він' form of the verb 'ма́ти', to have, which has the same spelling as 'ма́ти', mother, and is a different word: 'Він ма́є час.', he has time. Today 'нема́є' is one word, not a form of 'ма́ти' or of 'бу́ти'. For family and belongings, everyday Ukrainian prefers 'у ме́не є'.

'Є' is left out when the sentence describes what someone has instead of stating that it exists: 'У ме́не є сім’я́.' states that I have a family, while 'У ме́не вели́ка сім’я́.' describes it, I have a big family. A short answer can be 'Є.' alone: 'У те́бе є брат? Є.' The negative answer is 'Ні, нема́є.'

The personal pronouns have genitive forms of their own, shown in the table as they are said after a preposition. After any preposition, the forms of 'він', 'воно́', 'вона́' and 'вони́' begin with 'н': 'ньо́го', 'не́ї', 'них'. Without a preposition the same genitives are 'його́', 'її́' and 'їх', the forms you know as possessives: 'його́ брат', his brother, but 'у ньо́го є брат', he has a brother. 'Ме́не' and 'те́бе' are stressed on the first syllable after a preposition and on the last without one, as in the accusative 'Я тебе́ ба́чу.'

'У' with the genitive of a person also means at that person's home: 'Бабу́ся в ті́тки.', Grandma is at my aunt's. Five more prepositions take the genitive:

- 'без', without: 'ка́ва без цу́кру'
- 'для', for: 'кни́га для ма́ми'
- 'бі́ля', near, next to: 'бі́ля до́му'
- 'з', from: 'з Ки́єва', 'зі шко́ли'
- 'до', to, up to, until: 'до це́нтру', 'до ве́чора'

'З' meaning 'with' takes another case, the instrumental, as in 'ка́ва з молоко́м' (unit 4): one preposition with two meanings, each with its own case. 'До' with a person means to that person or to that person's home: 'Я йду до бабу́сі.', I am going to Grandma's. A place can take 'у' with the accusative (unit 13), into it, or 'до' with the genitive, up to it: 'Я йду в парк.' and 'Я йду до па́рку.' both mean 'I am going to the park'. 'До поба́чення' (unit 7) is 'до' with the genitive of 'поба́чення', a noun built on the verb for seeing: literally 'until seeing'. 'Бі́ля' always has a noun or pronoun after it, while the adverb 'по́руч' (unit 13) stands alone: 'Апте́ка бі́ля по́шти.', but 'Апте́ка по́руч.'

examples.source: Oksana doesn't have her key today.
The bank is near the railway station.

grammar.title: The vocative of family words
grammar.explanation:
The vocative (unit 7) is the form of a noun used to call or address someone. Ukrainians address the members of their family by family words as often as by name, so these words have vocatives in daily use, and they follow the rules you learned for first names:

- Feminine '-а' becomes '-о': 'ма́ма', 'ма́мо'; 'до́нька', 'до́нько'; 'ті́тка', 'ті́тко'.
- Feminine '-я' after a soft consonant becomes '-ю': 'бабу́ся', 'бабу́сю', like 'О́ля', 'О́лю'.
- Masculine '-о' becomes '-у': 'та́то', 'та́ту'; 'ба́тько', 'ба́тьку'; 'дя́дько', 'дя́дьку'.
- A masculine noun with a soft stem takes '-ю': 'діду́сь', 'діду́сю', like 'Андрі́й', 'Андрі́ю'.
- A masculine noun with a hard stem usually takes '-е': 'брат', 'бра́те', like 'Тара́с', 'Тара́се'.
- Before that '-е', 'г' becomes 'ж': 'друг', 'дру́же'. The same alternation turns 'к' into 'ч': 'чолові́к', 'чолові́че'.
- A few masculine nouns with a hard stem take '-у' instead, and 'син' is the one to know now: 'си́ну'.

The stress can move. 'Сестра́' is stressed on its ending, but its vocative 'се́стро' is stressed on the first syllable.

Use the vocative only for the person you speak to. A person you speak about stays in the nominative, so 'Ма́мо, де та́то?', Mom, where is Dad?, has 'ма́мо' for the listener and 'та́то' for the person talked about. Family vocatives are warm and very common: parents often say 'си́ну' or 'до́нько' to a child instead of the child's name, and children say 'ма́мо' and 'та́ту' to their parents. 'Ма́ти' and 'ба́тько' are more formal words, rarely used to call a parent at home.

culture.title: Family words and family ties
culture.text:
Grandparents have a central place in many Ukrainian families. They often live close by and look after the grandchildren while the parents work, and many children spend their summers with their grandparents in the countryside. The word for a village is 'село́'. The everyday words for grandparents, 'бабу́ся' and 'діду́сь', are affectionate forms: the plainer words are 'ба́ба' and 'дід', and the suffix '-ус-', with a soft 'с', adds warmth, as 'Grandma' and 'Grandpa' do in English. In the same way, parents are 'ма́ма' and 'та́то' in daily speech, while 'ма́ти' and 'ба́тько' are the neutral words of writing, of official forms and of respectful talk about someone else's parents.

Every Ukrainian has a patronymic, a name formed from the father's first name that follows a person's own first name. A man's patronymic ends in '-ович' or '-йович', a woman's in '-івна' or '-ївна'. Sam's teacher Іри́на Петрі́вна is the daughter of a man named 'Петро́', and a son of the same man has the patronymic 'Петро́вич'. First name and patronymic together, both in the vocative, are the polite way to address an older person or a teacher: 'Іри́но Петрі́вно'.

Address inside the family has changed over time. Most families today say 'ти' to parents and grandparents. In some villages and in some older families, children say 'ви' to their parents and grandparents as a sign of respect, with the vocative as usual: 'Ма́мо, ви вдо́ма?', Mom, are you at home? When you hear a grown son say 'ви' to his mother, it is a mark of tradition, not of distance.

exercises.prompt: Match the Ukrainian with the English
Which questions does the genitive answer?
exercises.explanation: The genitive answers 'кого́?', of whom, and 'чого́?', of what. 'Хто? що?' are the questions of the nominative.

exercises.prompt: Oksana calls her grandmother from the kitchen. Which form does she use?
exercises.explanation: To call or address someone, use the vocative. 'Бабу́ся' ends in '-я' after a soft consonant, so its vocative ends in '-ю'. 'Бабу́ся' is the nominative and 'бабу́сі' the genitive.

choices: I do not have a son.

exercises.audio_target: Сем із Кана́ди, а Окса́на з Ки́єва.
choices: Sam is from Canada, and Oksana is from Kyiv.
Sam is in Canada, and Oksana is in Kyiv.
Sam is from Kyiv, and Oksana is from Canada.

exercises.explanation: 'У ме́не є' states that something exists at me: 'є' is the verb, and 'син' is the subject.
'Без' takes the genitive. 'Молоко́' is neuter, and '-о' becomes '-а'.

exercises.prompt: Which genitive ending does a masculine noun naming a substance, such as 'сир' or 'цу́кор', usually take?
exercises.explanation: Substances usually take '-у' or '-ю': 'си́ру', 'цу́кру', 'ча́ю'. People, animals and things counted one by one take '-а' or '-я'.
You are speaking to your father, so 'та́то' is in the vocative: a masculine noun in '-о' takes '-у'.

choices: Our grandmother does not have a cat.

exercises.explanation: 'Бі́ля' takes the genitive. 'Парк' is a place, so it takes '-у'.

exercises.prompt: Why is the genitive of 'сестра́' 'сестри́', but the genitive of 'бабу́ся' 'бабу́сі'?
choices: 'Сестра́' has a hard stem, which takes '-и', and 'бабу́ся' a soft stem, which takes '-і'
The genitive of every family word ends in '-і'
exercises.explanation: Feminine nouns take '-и' after a hard stem and '-і' after a soft one. The 'с' of 'бабу́ся' is soft, as the 'я' shows.
After a preposition, the genitive of 'вона́' begins with 'н': 'у не́ї'. Without a preposition it is 'її́'.
'Бра́та' is in the genitive, so the possessive before it is too: 'мій' becomes 'мого́'.
'Чий' agrees with the thing owned. 'Ру́чка' is feminine, so the form is 'чия́'.

exercises.prompt_source: I am going to my brother's.
Coffee for Mom, and tea for Dad.

exercises.prompt: In 'У ме́не нема́є бра́та', why is 'бра́та' in the genitive?
choices: It is the subject of the sentence
'Нема́є' takes the genitive of what is absent
exercises.explanation: 'Нема́є' is a predicative word in a sentence without a subject, and the missing thing takes the genitive. In 'У ме́не є брат' the brother exists and is the subject, in the nominative.

exercises.prompt: Why does one say 'у ньо́го є брат' but 'його́ брат'?
choices: After a preposition, the genitive of 'він' begins with 'н'
exercises.explanation: 'Його́' and 'ньо́го' are the same genitive of 'він'. The form with 'н' is used after a preposition, here 'у'.

exercises.prompt: What is the genitive of 'ма́ти', mother?
exercises.explanation: 'Ма́ти' has a stem extension: its genitive is built on 'ма́тер-' and takes '-і', like 'сіль', 'со́лі'. 'Ма́ми' is the genitive of 'ма́ма'.

exercises.prompt: In this course's spelling, what tells 'сестри́', of the sister, apart from 'се́стри', sisters?
exercises.explanation: Both words have the same letters, and only the stress tells them apart. The genitive singular keeps the stress of 'сестра́' on the ending; the nominative plural moves it to the first syllable.
The owner follows 'у' in the genitive, so 'моя́ ті́тка' becomes 'моє́ї ті́тки', and 'син' is the subject. 'Моя́ ті́тка ма́є си́на.', with 'ма́є' and the accusative, is also correct.
'Нема́є' takes the genitive, and 'час' is an abstract idea, so it takes '-у'.
The owner follows the thing in the genitive. 'Оле́на' has a hard stem, so '-а' becomes '-и'.

exercises.prompt_source: The pharmacy is near the school.
exercises.explanation: 'Бі́ля' takes the genitive, and 'шко́ла' becomes 'шко́ли'. Ukrainian needs no word for 'is' here.
